gaps.text: Combining several spectroscopy methods (data fusion) (Low-level fusion of Raman and NIR spectra is a later hypothesis, not the first test. The probes must view the same medium or use a combined probe, data must be synchronised to a common time step, and each method needs its own calibration. The fused model must beat the best single method on held-out runs; otherwise drop the extra instrument.)
The supplied material does not give glucose or lactate detection limits, accuracy or response time for a cell-culture medium.
The supplied material does not specify a sterilizable or fouling-resistant probe installation for this cell-culture process.
The existing laboratory measurements are suitable as a reference for checking the in situ spectroscopy pilot.

items.finding: The review describes low-level data fusion as the simplest way to combine inputs by rearranging variables from different sources into one new data matrix.
items.how_it_applies: This could inform a first fusion test by defining a combined variable matrix, but the pilot should still compare the fused model against the best single method on held-out runs.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: The source is a review, not a cell-culture Raman/NIR study, and it does not establish that fusion improves glucose or lactate prediction in this process.

citation.quote: Low-level data fusion (LLDF) is considered the simplest method to achieve a combination of inputs. In this case, the data is rearranged into a new data matrix, where the variables coming from different sources are placed one after the other.
citation.label: E03 ¶31

items.finding: The review notes that in some situations instrument complementarity was not sufficient to improve prediction of several quality attributes, citing a Raman and FT-IR food study.
items.how_it_applies: This cautions that adding NIR to Raman should be justified by a held-out comparison against the best single method, rather than assumed from complementary instruments.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: The cited study is food analysis with Raman/FT-IR, not cell-culture Raman/NIR, so it does not predict performance for glucose or lactate here.

citation.quote: In some situations, instrument complementarity (not data complementarity) was not sufficient to improve the performance of predictive several CQAs, as shown by a Raman and FT-IR data based food analytical study [73].
citation.label: E03 ¶36

items.finding: Raman is described as frequently used in upstream processing because of high selectivity and low water interference, though measurement times are relatively long.
items.how_it_applies: This could support considering Raman for aqueous cell-culture medium, while prompting the pilot to record measurement time as a performance characteristic.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: The statement is general and does not report glucose or lactate detection limits, accuracy, or a numeric response time in cell-culture medium.

citation.quote: Raman spectroscopy is frequently applied in upstream processing in research and industry due to its high selectivity and low water interference [55] despite the relatively long measurement times.
citation.label: E02 ¶20
